item.title: Observation of collective flatbands in hybrid Mie-grating THz metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.28246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel type of functional metasurfaces created by a hybridization of Mie resonators with high-index optical gratings. We demonstrate that such hybrid metasurfaces possess flatbands characterized by zero group velocity and strong energy localization. We experimentally observe the flatbands in free-standing terahertz (THz) metasurfaces, where dielectric interconnections between Mie resonators, forming the grating, mediate multipolar hybridization and provide a geometric control over collective resonances. Our THz near-field measurements with a dipole excitation uncover long-lived coherent oscillations associated with the quasi-flat magnetic-dipolar resonant modes, while a spatial mapping resolves the resonant electromagnetic response across the dielectric interconnections. We vary the grating width continuously to tune the hybrid magnetic-dipolar resonances and substantially enhance the quality factor (Q factor), while preserving the quasi-!atband dispersion. Complementary Bloch-resolved Purcell calculations reveal the substantial Purcell enhancement with increasing Q factor, followed by a trend towards saturation and highlighting the interplay between radiative confinement and local emitter-mode coupling. We believe our findings establish the engineering of dielectric interconnections in periodic lattices as a novel strategy for spectrally tuning high-Q flatbands in these metastructures, tailoring localized electromagnetic interactions in functional optical metasurfaces.

item.title: Picojoule-level self-referencing with dual dispersive waves in thin-film lithium niobate
item.description: arXiv:2611.28304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate pulse-energy-efficient f-2f self-referencing of telecom-band pulses in a monolithic thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguide that combines Kerr spectral broadening with quasi-phase-matched (QPM) second-harmonic generation (SHG). Dispersion engineering generates dual dispersive waves (DWs) near 1 and 2 um, placed symmetrically around the pump to reduce the required spectral broadening. With an on-chip pulse energy of only 16.8 pJ, we detect a carrier-envelope-offset frequency (fceo) beatnote with a 32 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and we stabilize the fceo of an Er-fiber laser at 30 pJ, which is, to our knowledge, the lowest pulse energy reported for fceo stabilization at telecom wavelengths. Compared with an identical waveguide without poling, the QPM section enhances the beatnote SNR by 43 dB and reduces the required pulse energy fourfold. We further show that a mode-crossing DW, a chirped poling period, and a poled section aligned with the onset of DW generation to mitigate temporal walk-off are key to this performance.
item.dc:creator: Kiyoung Ko, Ian Christen, Kamila Kunes, Clayton Cheung, Chun-Ho Lee, Kiwon Kwon, Mihir Chaudhari, Ran Yin, Tushar Sanjay Karnik, Mengjie Yu

item.title: Cryogenic Luminescence Thermometry of Upconversion Micro- and Nanoparticles via Deep Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.28311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Luminescence thermometry with single or optically trapped particles is hampered by weak signals that fluctuate with alignment, collection efficiency, and excitation conditions and, for $\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$-based probes, by the loss of sensitivity of the luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) at cryogenic temperatures. Here we use a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) to predict the temperature directly from single emission spectra of $\mathrm{NaYF}_4{:}\mathrm{Yb}^{3+},\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ micro- and nanoparticles between $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $105\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and compare it with the standard LIR under adverse conditions deliberately reproduced with particle ensembles. From $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the 1D-CNN reduces the single-spectrum mean absolute error from $5.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $1.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and keeps its temperature uncertainty nearly constant down to the lowest temperatures, where Stark-component features remain temperature dependent while the LIR loses its sensitivity. Under deliberate optical misalignment, its error increases only from $0.58\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $0.88\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, whereas that of the LIR rises from $1.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $3.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The same approach reaches sub-degree accuracy ($0.21\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) over a narrow temperature window and a single calibration valid across different pump powers and wavelengths. These results establish 1D-CNNs as robust single-shot thermometers and a step toward fast thermometry of single and trapped particles.

item.title: Inverse design of polarization-analyzing gratings
item.description: arXiv:2611.28364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metasurface polarization analyzing gratings have attracted increasing interest for polarization management and sensing in optical systems. Traditional strategies for the design of these gratings are based on a formalism combining the Jones calculus with Fourier optics. While this approach has achieved notable success in numerous applications, its validity is restricted to the paraxial regime. Here we introduce a differentiable topology optimization framework for these gratings which is free of this constraint. We show that this framework can yield designs which outperform the traditional approach, especially at high angles. Additionally, we provide preliminary experimental validation to corroborate these results.
item.dc:creator: Kexin Bian, Alexander R. Fiani, Lisa W. Li, Noah A. Rubin

item.title: Excited-state lifetime and decay mechanisms in erbium-doped ZBLAN using Variable Excited-State dual-Pump Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.28398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a new technique for measuring excited-state lifetimes of rare-earth ions. This technique is particularly powerful for states that are very short lived or have a low photon yield because their de-excitation pathways are dominated by non-radiative processes. The technique uses dual optical parametric oscillators, whose pulses are separated by a variable delay. It reconstructs the excited-state decay curve from a series of delayed fluorescence intensity spectra rather than directly recording the fluorescence decay as done in conventional time-resolved laser fluorescence spectroscopy. The power of the technique is demonstrated by measuring the lifetime of the short-lived $^4I_{9/2}$ level in Er$^{3+}$-doped ZBLAN, which is well-known for its low photon yield. The technique enables accurate measurement of its lifetime and suggests a new depopulating mechanism involving the $^4I_{9/2}$ level in ZBLAN glass. Its accuracy is validated by measuring the lifetime of the $^4F_{9/2}$ state achieving excellent agreement with conventional time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy measurements. The approach is well suited for measuring lifetimes ranging from the sub-microsecond to the millisecond range. It provides a versatile platform for investigating excited-state dynamics and energy-transfer processes in RE-doped materials.

item.title: Anisoplanatic Blind Deconvolution using Phase Diversity
item.description: arXiv:2611.28458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence distorts the wavefront of light from a distant scene and blurs its image. Over a field of view wider than the isoplanatic angle, the distortion varies with direction and evolves in time, so no single wavefront describes the blur. Multiframe blind deconvolution (MFBD) can recover the scene from measurements spread over a long acquisition, but falls short during fast imaging because of limited diversity across measurements. We present coded anisoplanatic blind deconvolution (CA-BD), in which a pupil-plane spatial light modulator (SLM) applies a different known phase code to every measurement, with no wavefront sensor or deformable mirror, so that the measurements carry diversity even within a short acquisition. A per-pixel single-layer estimator recovers the object and spatially varying phases from the coded measurements. In simulation, a Cram\'er-Rao bound analysis shows that under anisoplanatism direct imaging needs about 41 times the photons of coded imaging for equal phase precision in strong turbulence. At the stronger of two turbulence strengths, CA-BD outperforms tuned MFBD on average at every burst length. It reduces the phase mean squared error 3.5x for stationary turbulence and 2-3x for time-varying turbulence. Measurements taken within a few coherence times benefit most from the known coded SLM patterns, making faster SLMs the key to its full advantage in time-varying turbulence.

item.title: MCP-based EUV ptychography with physics-simulation-trained residual learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.28912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microchannel-plate (MCP) detectors offer high gain for extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) experiments, but spatial blur and nonlinear response hinder quantitative diffraction imaging. Here, we present an MCP-based EUV ptychography system that combines detector hardware with physics-simulation-trained computational restoration. A residual-learning neural network trained on simulated detector degradation restores diffraction patterns without experimentally acquired training pairs. This preprocessing substantially improves image quality compared with reconstructions from uncorrected data under identical reconstruction settings. Single-harmonic imaging at $57$~nm yields an effective edge-response width of $1.08~\mu$m, approaching the nominal diffraction-limited scale of the imaging geometry. The approach further enables wavelength-multiplexed imaging at $44.4$ and $57$~nm. By coupling high-gain detection with computational compensation, this system enables high-resolution, multi-harmonic EUV ptychography and offers a cost-effective alternative to scientific-grade EUV CCD detectors

item.title: Multiscale wave-coupled neural networks for the inverse-design of broadband diffractive optics
item.description: arXiv:2611.28937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we introduce an inverse-design model called multiscale wave-coupled neural networks (MSWNets) inspired by physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that integrate the deep-learning capability of fully-connected neural networks with rigorous Rayleigh-Sommerfeld diffraction theory. MSWNets are trained using spatial input and output functions describing the height profiles of diffractive structures. Importantly, a MSWNet is composed of multiple sub-networks that provide learning across multiple frequency components of the optimal design solution. First, we validate and analyze the inverse design capabilities of the MSWNets' architecture through training on the complete complex field propagated from the analytical design of an axilens, demonstrating accurate reconstruction. Finally, we employ MSWNets, trained to maximize focusing efficiency, for the inverse design of novel diffractive devices. In particular, we design and display the performance of several achromatic lenses and doublets across the mid-wave infrared region ($3-5\rm{\;\mu} m$) with focal distance $f=500\rm{\;\mu m}$, demonstrating the potential of our inverse-design framework for the next-generation of broadband diffractive optical devices.
item.dc:creator: Peyton Brown, Riccardo Franchi, Roberto Riganti, Jonathan Schuster, Luca Dal Negro

item.title: A Candidate twin-spine photon model in MacCullagh's medium
item.description: arXiv:2611.29001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We model the vacuum as a rotationally elastic continuum, a low-energy electromagnetic approximation to the deformable spacetime metric of General Relativity. MacCullagh's single-parameter action yields the source-free Maxwell equations from resistance to twist, without separately postulating electric and magnetic fields. We show that a transversely localized field propagating rigidly at $c$ requires line defects; the minimal finite configuration is a twin-spine photon with two opposing displacement-current cores. It propagates without loss or transverse stress and admits linear and circular geometries with angular momentum $0$ or $\pm\hbar$. In a birefringent crystal, differential wave speeds reshape the shared spine trajectory, producing a continuous macroscopic torque without invoking superposed phase-delayed plane waves. For emission, we model the electron as a bound topological defect with a $\pi$-twist phase condition. Transverse acceleration shears its co-moving bow wave; the vacuum wave equation directs the residual dipole strain into twin-spine geometry, while the phase condition supplies a quantizing boundary condition. An accompanying SymPy Executable Research Record distinguishes postulated topology from derived mechanics.
item.dc:creator: B. Hou, D. A. Sinclair

item.title: Parallel Two-Photon Lithography: From Optical Nonlinearities to Energy Limits, Dose Control and Throughput Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2611.29010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-photon lithography (TPL) prints three-dimensional polymer architectures with sub-diffraction features, but writing them voxel by voxel limits its throughput. This review examines how parallelization overcomes this limit with fixed multi-focus arrays, reconfigurable holography using spatial light modulators and digital micromirror devices, hybrid metalens arrays, shaped beams, temporally focused projection and two-step absorption. An energy-deposition framework built on measured nonlinear absorption coefficients shows how the absorption order and coefficients of a resist determine its voxel size, energy per voxel and attainable voxel rate. Applied to parallel writing, the framework quantifies the costs of non-uniform foci, coherent crosstalk between foci, side-lobe losses in shaped beams and weaker axial confinement in projection. Published systems reach peak rates above $10^{8}$ voxels s$^{-1}$ with scanned focus arrays and up to $1.7\times10^{9}$ voxels s$^{-1}$ with grayscale projection under a fine-voxel definition, and parallel features as small as 20-55 nm. As rates rise, however, dose uniformity, proximity effects, heat, stitching and data bandwidth increasingly limit fidelity. A minimum reporting standard that includes the energy per voxel and sustained part-level rates is therefore proposed, together with priorities for the field: shared benchmark parts, predictive dose control and resists designed for parallel writing.
item.dc:creator: Michalis Stavrou, Panagiotis A. Loukakos, David Gray, Maria Farsari

item.title: Efficient phase-only wavefront shaping at 250 kHz for multimode fiber endomicroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.29015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wavefront shaping through multimode fibers (MMFs) enables diffraction-limited fluorescence imaging with hair-thin probes, at a speed and light budget bounded by the wavefront modulator. Existing modulators provide at most two of three key characteristics: high refresh rate, (high) modal dimensionality, and light efficiency. Here, we demonstrate wavefront control through an MMF using a tailored phase-only microelectromechanical modulator that combines all three, with 8,192 elements arranged in a 32 x 256 array, 7-bit phase control, and a 250 kHz full-frame refresh rate. Direct on-axis phase modulation delivers 70+/-5% of the incident light into the modulated field and eliminates both off-axis encoding optical losses and hologram computation. The generated foci at the distal end of the fiber remain isotropic with high fidelity. We use singular-value decomposition analysis of the measured transmission to identify the effective degrees of freedom of our system. By scanning the focus at multiple depths, we demonstrate volumetric fluorescence imaging. These results open a new operating regime for adaptive in vivo multimode-fiber endoscopy.

item.title: Optical Motion Sensing for Piezoelectric-Resonator-Based Power Converters
item.description: arXiv:2611.29035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Piezoelectric components present a promising alternative to conventional magnetics for miniaturized, high-frequency power converters. While high-Q piezoelectric resonators have demonstrated high efficiencies and large power densities in prototype high-frequency dc-dc converters, their optimal operating conditions are sensitive to temperature fluctuations and load variations. Therefore, robust closed-loop control is essential for practical deployment. Electrical approaches for sensing motional current may compromise the electrical isolation and electromagnetic interference (EMI) immunity inherently provided by the mechanical nature of these resonators. Here, we present an optical motion sensing approach for piezoelectric power converters. The optical sensing system comprises a laser, fiber optics, and a photodetector. The proposed approach uses optical interference to monitor the mechanical displacement in real time. The resulting optical signal carries both the amplitude and phase of the mechanical motion, which are necessary for closed-loop control. We experimentally characterize and validate this optical motion sensing approach using a 45-kHz piezoelectric resonator driven by a GaN half bridge with input voltages up to 45 V. We further experimentally demonstrate closed-loop control using the proposed optical motion sensing for a 99-kHz isolated piezoelectric converter. These initial results establish a viable pathway toward optically closed-loop control of piezoelectric power converters.
item.dc:creator: Liyang Jin, Zhiyang Cao, Jun Ji, Liyan Zhu, Linbo Shao

item.title: Uniguided and unicoupled resonances in an asymmetric acoustic metasurface
item.description: arXiv:2611.29078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically study an acoustic metasurface that exhibits ultimate asymmetry in absorption under oblique incidence. This behavior arises from a counter-propagating pair of uniguided (UGR) and unicoupled (UCR) resonances. The UGR radiates to only one side, while the UCR radiates to both sides but can be excited from only one. In the lossless regime, the transmission phase winds by $2\pi$ across both UCR and UGR while the transmittance remains flat at any prescribed nonzero level. Thermoviscous losses introduce resonant intensity modulation and enable critical coupling, yielding perfect sound absorption exclusively for incidence through the channel that excites the UCR. Therefore, asymmetric metasurfaces with UCR and UGR offer a route to full phase control and perfect sound absorption.
item.dc:creator: Andrey S. Konchakov, Daniil S. Buzin, Dmitrii N. Maksimov, Mingzhao Song, Y. Li, Mikhail I. Petrov, Chao Peng, Andrey A. Bogdanov, Pavel S. Pankin

item.title: Acoustic bound states in the continuum in a labyrinthine meta-atom
item.description: arXiv:2611.29091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this Letter, we theoretically and experimentally study acoustic bound states in the continuum (BICs) emerging in labyrinth meta-atom embedded in an acoustic waveguide. A symmetry-protected BIC is supported in the lossless limit when the meta-atom is positioned on the waveguide axis. Breaking the symmetry by shifting the meta-atom away from the center of the waveguide transforms the BIC into a radiative quasi-BIC, manifested by the emergence of a narrow resonant feature in the transmittance spectrum. The proposed concept is experimentally tested using a 3D-printed labyrinthine meta-atom placed inside an impedance tube. The measured transmittance spectra are consistent with numerical simulations and support the BIC-to-quasi-BIC transition induced by symmetry breaking in the presence of thermoviscous losses. The resonance frequency, contrast, and linewidth can be controlled by varying the meta-atom position. The observed behavior is interpreted within a two-mode temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT), providing an analytical description of the resonant response. The ability to tune radiative leakage in the presence of absorption makes the proposed acoustic BIC platform promising for the development of tunable absorbers, sensors, and modulators.
item.dc:creator: Aleksandra S. Zheleznova, Iuliia A. Timankova, ZiWei Ye, Yunmeng Wang, Jihao Tang, Mikhail V. Kuzmin, Nikolay S. Solodovchenko, Mihail I. Petrov, Andrey A. Bogdanov, Pavel S. Pankin, Yong Li

item.title: Reconfigurable Microwave Photonic All-Pass Filters based on Optical Kerr Microcombs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microwave photonic (MWP) all pass filters (APFs), which enable phase manipulation without altering signal amplitudes, are essential for phase engineering in high bandwidth microwave signal processing. However, achieving a high degree of reconfigurability in the filter order and characteristic parameters of APFs remains challenging for conventional methods. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a new strategy for realizing MWP APFs based on a microcomb driven transversal filter system, enabling high reconfigurability, sharp phase transitions with high group delays, and low loss. We experimentally demonstrate both 1st and 2nd order APFs, achieving a maximum amplitude variation (MAV) of 1.95 dB and a maximum group delay (MGD) of 580 ps for the former, and a MAV of 2.01 dB and an MGD of 1740 ps for the latter. In addition, both independent and joint tuning of APF characteristic parameters are demonstrated by simply programming the tap coefficients without changing any hardware, enabling highly reconfigurable filter response for diverse phase engineering functionalities. These results highlight the potential of our approach for implementing MWP APFs with both high performance and reconfigurability for practical applications requiring dynamic and versatile phase control.

item.title: 2D MXene integrated optical polarizers based on TiO2 with high performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.29121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, two dimensional (2D) materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D material based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO2). The 2D TiO2 exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal / chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers to achieve a record high polarizer FOM of 17.5 (among 2D material-coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield ( 98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios up to 12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong capability for large-scale manufacturing, these polarizers represent a solid step towards industry ready implementations of 2D material based optical polarizers.

item.title: Polarization-independent self-hybridized strong coupling by Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum in bulk WS2 metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.29204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-refractive-index dielectric metasurfaces supporting optical modes are ideal candidates for achieving strong coupling with transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) materials. However, optical illumination with a specific polarization is always required to estimate the maximal coupling strength in such coupled systems due to the polarization-dependent optical modes. Here, we propose a self-hybridized strong coupling between Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum (BZF-QBICs) mode and A excitons in the same bulk WS2 metasurface. By changing the thickness of the bulk WS2 metasurfaces, a typical anticrossing behavior with Rabi splitting of 165.9 meV is observed. Such Rabi splitting is unchanged when changing the polarization of the incident light from linearly to circularly polarizations, demonstrating the polarization-independent self-hybridized strong coupling. This work provides a novel method for realizing robust polarization-independent polaritons in bulk TMDCs metasurface and offers new insights for expanding the applications of polaritonic devices with arbitrary polarizations.
item.dc:creator: Xiongwei Guo, Fu Liu, Jinhai Si, Xun Hou, Kuidong Wang

item.title: Giant thermal transduction via feedback-phase engineering in a thin-film lithium-niobate opto-electro-mechanical oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2611.29263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional resonant MEMS thermometry typically relies on the intrinsic temperature coefficient of frequency (TCF) of mechanical resonances. Here we show that embedding a suspended thin-film lithium-niobate mechanical resonator in an opto-electro-mechanical (OEM) feedback loop enhances the intrinsic coefficient by two orders of magnitude. By using laser--cavity detuning to control the loop's round-trip phase, and thus the Barkhausen-selected oscillation frequency, we engineer an effective TCF of $+1.24\times10^{4}$~ppm/K: a 100-fold enhancement and a sign reversal relative to its intrinsic TCF of $-124$~ppm/K. Temperature-dependent and open-loop phase measurements confirm that this giant response originates from feedback phase selection rather than from the passive resonator itself. This interpretation is further supported by the independently measured closed-loop oscillation frequencies and a detuning-dependent delay model. The same architecture also supports 2:1 subharmonic injection locking, yielding sub-6~Hz linewidths, reference-limited frequency stability, and tunable operation from $76.71$ to $76.82$~MHz. These results establish feedback-phase engineering as a general, post-fabrication route to both giant thermal transduction and low-noise yet tunable mechanical oscillation.
item.dc:creator: Ran Yin, Yue Yu, Ian Christen, Mengjie Yu

item.title: Ultrabroadband, high-sensitivity time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy enabled by a Yb-based laser system
item.description: arXiv:2611.29295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultrafast optical fields have introduced numerous novel light-induced states in quantum materials. Identifying these states and elucidating their formation mechanisms require comprehensive, quantitative access to nonequilibrium electrodynamics across relevant energy scales. Here, we develop a Yb-laser-based time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy (TRTS) platform combining multi-pass-cell pulse compression, spintronic terahertz generation, and air-biased coherent detection. A single time-domain waveform scan provides continuous phase-resolved spectral coverage to 25 THz ($\sim$100 meV) with a Fourier resolution of 0.1 THz ($\sim$0.4 meV). This capability enables the characterization of both low-frequency charge dynamics and higher-energy resonant excitations in quantum materials under a common temporal reference. The system achieves a single-scan time-domain signal-to-noise ratio of 72 dB with long-term waveform stability, while preserving most of the laser pulse energy for tunable excitation. Measurements on intrinsic GaAs resolve extremely weak phonon features above 23 THz and demonstrate quantitative retrieval of equilibrium and transient complex optical properties. The resulting platform can provide a more complete microscopic picture of light-induced states in quantum materials.
item.dc:creator: Hong-Yuan Wu, Si-Jia Li, Jing-Long Ma, Guo-Qian Liao, Alexander Holm Ohrt, Long Cheng, Peter Uhd Jepsen, Bin-Bin Zhou, Si-Jie Zhang, Yu-Tong Li

item.title: Turbulence Strength Estimation from Multiplexed Orbital Angular Momentum Beams Using Multimode Fibre Speckle
item.description: arXiv:2611.29382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The strength of atmospheric turbulence governs how much the modes of a free-space optical link mix together. It is usually measured with a separate instrument or with a Gaussian probe beam, neither of which uses the beams that a structured-light link already carries. Here we show that the turbulence strength, expressed as the Fried parameter, can be estimated directly from multiplexed orbital angular momentum (OAM) beams without knowing which modes are present. The beams pass through a passive multimode fibre that turns them into speckle on a camera, and a trained weighted sum of the camera pixels (known as an extreme learning machine), averaged over a few tens of frames, gives the Fried parameter. In the laboratory with emulated turbulence, superpositions of up to eleven OAM modes give an estimate as accurate as that from a Gaussian probe beam sent through the same fibre. In all but weak turbulence the estimate is also more accurate than an ideal Strehl meter or an ideal tip/tilt sensor, providing an efficient way to estimate turbulence strength in mode-division multiplexed systems.
item.dc:creator: Warwick G. C. Brown, Mitchell A. Cox

item.title: Polarization-cloaked spatiotemporal topological knots
item.description: arXiv:2611.29498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatiotemporally localized topological knots encode global connectivity within a moving space-time optical wavepacket, circumventing the requirement for spatial-only eigenmodes that extend throughout three-dimensional space-filling. In conventional modalities, this connectivity is identified directly from a scalar complex field. However, knotting optical knots with the polarization state of light proves difficult to realize for ultrafast localized wavepackets. In this work, we combine oppositely wound toroidal vortex modes with orthogonal circular polarization states on the higher-order Poincar\'e sphere to construct vectorial electromagnetic spatiotemporal wavepackets, in which the topological connectivity is encoded in the relative phase between the polarization components. Stokes analysis shows that S_0 retains a common toroidal envelope, whereas the phase sensitive Stokes parameters S_1 and S_2 reveal winding-dependent linked and knotted trajectories; numerical simulations verify their closure, and time-sliced off-axis interferometry experimentally reconstructs the corresponding three-dimensional S_2 textures. This separation of topological connectivity from the scalar intensity envelope extends the control of spatiotemporal topology to the polarization degree of freedom and provides a versatile framework for controlling how topological information is accessed in multidimensional structured light.
item.dc:creator: Yaning Zhou, Nianjia Zhang, Zhao Zhang, Chunhao Liang, Qian Cao, Houan Teng, Qiwen Zhan, Sergey A. Ponomarenko, Xu Guo, Yangjian Cai, Xin Liu

item.title: Pseudo-Altermagnetism in Non-Hermitian Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Altermagnetism has attracted growing attention, and its analogs have been actively explored across classical platforms. Here, we introduce pseudo-altermagnetism in non-Hermitian systems, where balanced gain and loss plays the role of the altermagnetic spin, and the opposite gain and loss sublattices are related by an antiunitary symmetry $O$ with $O\bm k\neq \bm k$ for generic momentum $\bm k$. Using a two-dimensional non-Hermitian system with $O=C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$ symmetry as a representative example, we find that pseudo-altermagnetism not only leads to a momentum-dependent gain and loss distribution analogous to the momentum-dependent spin splitting of altermagnets, but also exhibits intrinsic non-Hermitian properties. The bands of $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$-invariant non-Hermitian systems are either isolated or paired by $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$, and both cases are guaranteed to host movable but unremovable nodal structures, characterized by the zeros of two distinct quantities. An isolated band exhibits two movable but unremovable Hermitian spectral lines, whose generic points are not invariant under $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$, in sharp contrast to the conventional Hermitian spectra enforced only at the fixed points of an antiunitary symmetry. The paired bands, in turn, feature a movable but unremovable nodal network formed by the union of real-part and imaginary-part degeneracy lines, whose intersections are generally exceptional points. We further demonstrate these findings in a non-Hermitian photonic crystal. Our results establish a symmetry-based bridge between non-Hermitian physics and altermagnetism, and provide novel mechanisms of Hermitian spectra beyond $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry.
item.dc:creator: Chang-Yin Ji, Runze Li, Zhi-Ming Yu, Yugui Yao

item.title: Designing Incoherent Multispectral Diffractive Optical Networks for Satellite Image Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.30079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These advantages are especially attractive for multispectral satellite imaging, where conventional workflows rely on transmitting high-dimensional image cubes to the ground for downstream electronic analysis. Here, we introduce a computationally efficient surrogate model-guided framework for designing incoherent multispectral diffractive optical networks that directly output class probabilities onboard, eliminating the need to capture and transfer the full multispectral data cube for ground-side inference. We first train a physically compatible surrogate model, represented by a non-negative fully connected model that accommodates a generalized detector readout, yielding a task-specific non-negative multispectral intensity transformation that can be transferred to an optical processor. We then synthesize its diffractive counterpart through data-free point-spread-function-based optimization under spatially incoherent illumination. Using this approach, we numerically demonstrate a six-spectral-channel diffractive classifier for tri-class satellite-scene recognition, achieving a blind-testing accuracy of 79.8% for artificial surface, water body, and vegetated land images, closely approaching the 81.8% accuracy of its surrogate. We further demonstrate a more compact three-spectral-channel design that numerically achieves 72.7% blind-testing accuracy, compared with 75.1% for its corresponding surrogate model. This surrogate model-guided strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compact, task-specific incoherent multispectral optical processors for resource-constrained remote-sensing inference.

item.title: Strain-driven terahertz phase modulation in piezoelectric and nonlinear optical crystals: mechanisms, material developments, and modulation strategies
item.description: arXiv:2611.30194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terahertz (THz) technology has witnessed notable developments in sensing, spectroscopy, imaging, and wireless communication which have increased the demand for high-performance THz modulators. Among the various approaches for controlling the THz waves, the application of external stimuli such as optical pumping and thermal or electric fields is widely employed as a promising strategy for modulation. This review focuses on recent advances in THz modulation based on different materials including 2D semiconductors and metamaterials with attention to their response under external stimuli. In addition, strain-driven THz modulation in non-centrosymmetric piezoelectric materials including organic and semi-organic crystals is examined with an emphasis on their ability to establish strong coupling between propagating THz waves and lattice vibrations under piezoelectric resonance conditions. We further highlight earlier reports on strain-driven THz modulation in lithium niobate (LiNbO3) and critically assess the potential of several other nonlinear optical crystals exhibiting piezoelectric resonance peaks suitable for strain-driven THz modulation. An overview of THz modulators integrated with tunable materials is presented highlighting their operating principles and key performance metrics comprising modulation speed, bandwidth, modulation depth and insertion loss.
item.dc:creator: Aarifa Muhammed Ashraf, Rajaboopathi Mani

item.title: Polarization switching of double azimuthal backflow in two transverse orbital angular momentum superpositions
item.description: arXiv:2611.30213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical backflow in the azimuthal direction can be generated by the interference of two rotating-wave structured light beams with distinct transverse topological charges and equal intensity. Here we show that the interference reverses both azimuthal components of the Poynting and the canonical momenta. Although these two momenta are not generally tied, they reverse jointly here: both acquire azimuthal backflow in a common angular sector, while their radial intervals can differ. The double backflow is switched solely by the polarizations of the two beams, without amplitude tuning. A single polarization overlap enters the interference terms of both momenta but not the single-beam terms of either, so that matched polarizations switch the double backflow on whereas mismatched ones switch it off. The double backflow is periodic in the azimuthal direction, with its angular period locked to the topological charge difference and independent of the individual charges. Our results establish a vectorial mechanism for polarization-gated azimuthal backflow, with potential applications in polarization-switchable optical manipulation.
item.dc:creator: Zhen-Lai Wang

item.title: Computation in flight through precision-processed optical fiber
item.description: arXiv:2611.30266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In distributed sensing and computing systems, optoelectronic conversion, buffering, and scheduling can make data movement a bottleneck. We propose FBG-CA, a passive computing module fabricated by automated through-coating inscription of weak fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs). The spatially distributed FBGs reflect, delay, and accumulate temporal samples to produce a convolution output in the backward direction, while the forward signal carries the original data stream to a remote receiver. This enables transmission and convolution within the same optical propagation event. To mitigate finite reflectivity resolution and fabrication deviations, we combine quantization-aware training with sharpness-aware minimization. Over 1440 m of computing fiber, the single-wavelength implementation achieves a convolution correlation coefficient of 0.987, classification accuracies of 87.90% on MNIST and 79.07% on MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, and an estimated throughput of 288 GOPS. With approximately 20% forward-power reduction (0.97 dB) across the FBG sections, the recovered MNIST images achieve a mean structural similarity index of 0.9930, and the recovered MIT-BIH heartbeat waveforms have a mean squared error of 0.005826. Using four wavelength-division-multiplexed channels over 144 m of computing fiber, FBG-CA achieves 92.25% accuracy on four-class Fashion-MNIST and an estimated throughput of 115.2 GOPS. An architecture-level projection indicates an intrinsic throughput density of 1.6 POPS/m for eight wavelengths at 100 GBaud per wavelength. These results demonstrate passive, wavelength-scalable computation-in-flight in optical fiber.
item.dc:creator: Kailai Liu, Zhongyao Luo, Xiangpeng Xiao, Zhen Wang, Weiliang Zhao, Mingming Zhang, Hao Wu, Zhijun Yan, Ming Tang

item.title: SPECTRA-RCWA: A Spectral Propagation Engine for Coupled-Wave Theory with Recursive Admittance
item.description: arXiv:2611.30305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) is the standard full-wave solver for periodic metasurfaces, but every solve diagonalises a dense nonsymmetric matrix for each layer. Inverse design repeats this step for every wavelength, angle and polarisation of an objective. On a graphics processor it is the slow step, and its derivative fails where eigenvalues coincide or a diffraction order reaches cutoff. Here we introduce SPECTRA-RCWA, an RCWA forward and adjoint solver that never diagonalises the layer matrix. Each layer step uses three entire functions of the half-size layer matrix, evaluated by matrix products alone, and an admittance recursion, or scattering-matrix doubling for thick layers, keeps the evanescent orders stable. One adjoint field gives the gradient for every design value without a computational graph, and all solves of an objective run as one batch. For 144 solves with 578 x 578 layer matrices, the value and the gradient take 0.25 s on one graphics card, 218 times less than with a differentiable eigendecomposition code. The truncated-series solver TorchRDIT loses accuracy beyond a few tenths of a micrometre unless the user slices the layer; SPECTRA-RCWA keeps single-precision accuracy in layers several wavelengths thick with no setting changed and is 47 to 65 times faster at matched accuracy. Its single-precision gradient stays within 4e-5 of a double-precision reference at a cutoff, where eigendecomposition gradients are wrong by order one. A freeform metagrating designed in 3.4 min on a desktop processor deflects both polarisations by 65 degrees with a band-averaged efficiency of 75%.
item.dc:creator: Hyoseok Park

item.title: Dark and bright solitons in a multimodal lithium tantalate microresonator
item.description: arXiv:2611.30313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bright-soliton and dark-pulse microcombs provide complementary outputs. Integrating both states in a single resonator would expand the operating capabilities of an integrated coherent source, but requires opposite group-velocity-dispersion (GVD) channels while reconciling localized interfamily interaction for dark-pulse formation with spectral isolation for independent bright-soliton pumping. Wavelength-addressed access to both states is achieved in a LiTaO$_3$ microring through two TE-like transverse mode families. The higher-order TE$_{10}$ family fulfills two distinct roles in different spectral regions. Within localized avoided-mode-crossing regions, mode-resolved spectroscopy implicates TE$_{10}$ in perturbing the normal-GVD TE$_{00}$ resonance sequence. Away from these regions, TE$_{10}$ retains anomalous GVD and remains spectrally isolated as an independently pumpable bright-soliton channel; at representative pump resonances, the closest resonance of the non-addressed family is separated by 75--192 loaded cavity linewidths. With the input polarization held fixed, pumping TE$_{00}$ and TE$_{10}$ resonances generates dark-pulse and bright-soliton microcombs, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental realization of a dark-pulse microcomb in an integrated LiTaO$_3$ microring. These results establish transverse-mode-family engineering as a route to combining localized modal interaction with independent spectral addressing in a single microresonator.
item.dc:creator: Huizong Zhu, Yuyao Guo, Xiangfei Cheng, Yiqun Wu, Juanjuan Lu

item.title: Equivalence and origin of discrepancies between transfer matrix method and multiple reflection model of surface induced second harmonic generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Second harmonic generation (SHG) spectroscopy is a sensitive tool to study surfaces and interfaces in thin films. To understand the layer boundaries and interpret the measured data, it is essential to use a theoretical model describing the SHG generation in the thin film. The transfer matrix method and multiple reflection model are two numerical techniques which have been commonly utilized in the calculation of surface-induced SHG. Here, we demonstrate that, despite the expected equivalence of the approaches, the two methods can lead to controversial results for the same input properties and second-order susceptibility tensors. The discrepancies resulting in different SHG intensity from both methods are caused by inconsistent numerical implementation of the interface SHG. We describe the conditions for the implementation to achieve the equivalence between the two models. Moreover, we identify the physical constraint that has to be imposed in numerical implementation to get identical results from both methods.
item.dc:creator: Deependra Singh Gaur, Jakub Luke\v{s}, Karel \v{Z}\'idek

item.title: 1.2 dB Insertion Loss in a Monolithically Integrated Silicon Mach-Zehnder Optical Isolator Using Stoichiometric Ce:YIG
item.description: arXiv:2611.30501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated optical isolators play a crucial role in photonic integrated circuits (PICs) by effectively stabilizing optical signals, making them indispensable components for advanced photonic systems. However, integrated magneto-optical (MO) isolators suffer from their high insertion loss, which is mainly caused by the relatively low FoM of Ce:YIG MO thin films deposited on silicon. Here, we show that film stoichiometry plays a key role in controlling the FoM of Ce:YIG. We observed garnet phase Fe-rich and Ce-rich nano-clusters in non-stoichiometric Ce:YIG. By using an iron-deficient target, we demonstrated that nearly stoichiometric Ce:YIG films on Si(100) could be fabricated, eliminating the nano-cluster defects. Consequently, the film exhibited a saturation Faraday rotation angle of -5523 deg/cm and a figure of merit of 72.7 deg/dB, which is 1.7 times higher compared to nonstoichiometric films. An MZI-type optical isolator on SiN fabricated by this method demonstrated a record low insertion loss of 1.2 dB and isolation ratio of 27.6 dB at 1556 nm wavelength. Our results provide an important step toward the practical application of integrated MO nonreciprocal photonic devices.

item.title: Motion of dissipative solitons in quasi-one-dimensional potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.30594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the motion of two-dimensional (2D) dissipative solitons and soliton pairs in the framework of the cubic-quintic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation with quasi-1D potentials, spatially periodic or radial-lattice ones. The equation is solved numerically for inputs representing one or two fundamental solitons, which are set in motion by a kick. For the quasi-1D potential, the kick parallel to the potential axis naturally initiates free motion of the 2D solitons, as the model remains Galilean-invariant in this direction. Motion in the transverse direction, which may entail pulse multiplication, commences if the kick is strong enough. Oblique kicks lead to a straightforward superposition of the longitudinal and transverse motions. Also considered is the collision between 2D solitons moving in the longitudinal and diagonal directions. In the radial potential, the soliton kicked towards the center may bounce back from the central potential hill or pass it, producing complex trajectories and splitting of the moving soliton.
item.dc:creator: Valentin Besse, Herv{\'e} Leblond, Dumitru Mihalache, Boris A. Malomed

item.title: A Highly Tunable (Ti,Zr)N$_x$-Based MIM Plasmonic Sensor for Multidomain Biological, Chemical, and Physical Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2611.30614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metal-Insulator-Metal (MIM) plasmonic refractive index (RI) sensors have attracted considerable attention for label-free, real-time analyte detection; however, their reliance on noble metals such as gold and silver imposes fundamental constraints on tunability, thermal stability, and CMOS process compatibility. In this work, we propose a novel MIM plasmonic RI sensor based on a square ring resonator with embedded circular nanorods, employing the ternary nitride (Ti,Zr)N$_x$ as the plasmonic material, marking its first application in a MIM sensing platform. Compared to binary nitrides and other alternative plasmonic materials reported in the literature, (Ti,Zr)N$_x$ offers broader compositional tunability and greater flexibility in tailoring the optical response while remaining fully CMOS-compatible. The sensor is validated across a comprehensive range of biosensing and physicochemical analyte scenarios, including glucose monitoring for diabetes assessment, hemoglobin-based anemia classification across four severity levels, simultaneous discrimination of five major blood constituents, and cancer cell identification across six tissue types. For physical and chemical sensing, the structure achieves an air pressure sensitivity of 6.158 nm/MPa with negligible thermal cross-sensitivity, and a CO$_2$ detection sensitivity of 330.12 pm/ppm via polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) functionalization, which is the highest reported among comparable structures in the literature. The proposed sensor achieves a maximum RI sensitivity of 2146.496 nm/RIU with a detection limit of $4.669 \times 10^{-7}$ RIU, outperforming previously reported CMOS-compatible plasmonic RI sensors.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Abrar Kabir, Aosaf Jarif Siddiquee, Abdullah Taharat, A. K. M. Rakib, Rakibul Hasan Sagor

item.title: Pulse-to-pulse Power Fluctuations in Ultra-Fast Fiber Amplifiers with Gain-Managed Nonlinearity
item.description: arXiv:2611.30794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical framework for predicting pulse-to-pulse power fluctuations caused by pump and seed power noise and by amplified spontaneous emission in ultrafast fiber amplifiers operating in the gain-managed nonlinear regime. The numerical model evaluates statistically averaged quantities directly, without Monte Carlo simulations with stochastic sources, and reduces to a semi-analytical monochromatic model in the limit of vanishing signal bandwidth and negligible ASE. We show that nonlinear spectral broadening of the signal and of its perturbations, combined with the frequency-dependent gain, significantly alters the technical relative intensity noise in both the high-power, high-repetition-rate and the low-power, low-repetition-rate regimes, and that in the latter regime the contributions related to amplified spontaneous emission become comparable to those induced by pump and seed fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Maksim Kozlov, Colin J. McKinstrie, Nitzan Haviv, Pavel Sidorenko

item.title: Programmable Broadband Polarization-Preserving Optical Delay Line with Faraday Mirrors
item.description: arXiv:2611.30814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report a broadband optical delay line programmable for delays up to 1 {\mu}s with nanosecond resolution, while preserving an arbitrary and unknown polarization state of the original light. The delay line comprises bidirectional pass in cascaded segments of standard single-mode fibers, along with terminal reflection from Faraday mirrors (FMs) at both ends. Each segment contains either a short path or a long path, selected by an optical switch. The FMs auto-compensate for random polarization fluctuations introduced by the optical fibers, thereby restoring the initial polarization state. Broadband operation of the delay line was assessed by investigating dispersion of both the fiber and the FMs. Surprisingly, we found that the two-pass propagation in the fiber can mitigate dispersive distortion introduced by the FM. Numerical experiments demonstrated that the output polarization state of the delay line has a mean fidelity better than 99% over a range of 50-nm deviation from the central wavelength. Remarkably, the mean fidelity often surpasses that in the absence of the fiber itself.

item.title: Localized Strain Tuning of Second-Harmonic Generation in MoS2 Monolayers and Bilayers
item.description: arXiv:2611.31097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the modulation of second-harmonic generation (SHG) in CVD-grown MoS2 monolayers and few-layer flakes through localized mechanical deformation applied by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip. MoS2 membranes suspended over microstructured Si3N4 substrates allow simultaneous measurements of force and SHG intensity during controlled approach and retraction cycles. Suspended regions exhibit enhanced SHG relative to substrate-supported regions, with pronounced suppression near the clamping boundaries. While the SHG response during compressive loading varies among individual membranes, adhesion-mediated pulling during retraction consistently reduces the SHG intensity until tip detachment, when the signal recovers. By correlating the optical modulation with the measured pull-off force and a phenomenological estimate of effective strain, we obtain a characteristic sensitivity of approximately 12% SHG modulation per 1% effective strain, with comparable behavior in monolayers and bilayers. These findings reveal adhesion-mediated mechanical deformation as a distinct and reversible mechanism for controlling nonlinear optical emission in atomically thin membranes.
item.dc:creator: Mart\'in Aversa, Florencia Cammarata, Camila Borraz\'as, Nadia C. Vega, David Comedi, Andrea V. Bragas, Gustavo Grinblat

item.title: HEP-like 1550 nm wide-field pixelated optical receiver for inter-satellite laser links: a simulation-based proof of concept for Earth, lunar and Earth-Moon scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2611.28071v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: I propose and evaluate by simulation a wide-field dome optical receiver (a field of view larger than a hemisphere) at 1550 nm for the acquisition of inter-satellite laser links. The detector is an InGaAs pixel hybrid of about 1 Mpixel with event-driven, time-stamped readout, inspired by the pixel detectors of high-energy physics. A pulsed beacon is detected by the coincidence of m hits in a sliding block of pixels, and the angle of arrival (AoA) is estimated by clustering and centroiding and handed to a narrow-field data channel. In a 550 km Earth constellation, with a 5 mrad beacon and a 10 mm aperture, detection takes 12 $\mu$s to 2 ms (up to 116 ms with the 6-9 mm that the optics allow), with a whole-frame false-alarm rate below 0.01/s, and the AoA error is 0.13-0.23 mrad. Cooling to about 233 K gives a service life above 5 years for fluences up to about $2\times10^{9}$ p/cm$^2$ per year. The receiver is also studied around the Moon and on the Earth-Moon link, where it works only between high orbits. Compared phase by phase with published scan-based acquisition, the search phase (3-18 ms with 10 mm) is shorter by a factor of about $10^{2}$ to $10^{5}$; end to end, with assumed pointing and loop-closure times, it takes 0.16-1.5 s, comparable to a terminal with calibrated open-loop pointing but without requiring that pointing at the receiver; the partner's beacon must still be pointed at it to about 1.25 mrad (5 mrad beacon). All values are simulation results, obtained with idealised optics and a 1 Mpixel detector that does not exist today; none is a measurement.
item.dc:creator: Maurizio De Santis

item.title: photon number correlations in harmonics driven with classical and quantum light
item.description: arXiv:2611.28498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent reports of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised questions about whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily imply genuinely quantum behaviour. Here, we compare the low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical and bright squeezed vacuum sources. The latter generates strong auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and heralding measurements show that the cross-correlations are fully classical and can be explained by the common fluctuations from the driving field. A visible scaling of the measured correlation function with mean harmonic flux is observed, which is well-explained by a click detector-response model.
item.dc:creator: Katarzyna M. Kowalczyk, Michael T. Weil, Kevin Murzyn, Andr\'e Staudte, Jeff S. Lundeen, David M. Villeneuve, Giulio Vampa

item.title: Handed Ultrafast Dynamics in Chiral Cyanine Nanotubes
item.description: arXiv:2611.28973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We detect helicity-dependent excited state relaxation in a chiral exciton system. Using L-histidine as a chiral inducer, we prepared unbundled, double-walled J-aggregrate nanotubes of an amphiphilic cyanine dye with a net handedness, which gives a large circular dichroism dissymmetry factor ($g_{abs} = 3.6 \times 10^{-2}$). With two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy and circularly polarized pump pulses, we find that the relaxation rates of longitudinal excitons depend on pump helicity (4.5 $ps^{-1}$ for $\langle \textit{RRXX} \rangle$ vs 6 $ps^{-1}$ for $\langle \textit{LLXX} \rangle$, a difference of about 30%) and is the same in the inner and outer tubes. Transverse excitons show no significant dependence. Chirality and pump helicity therefore bias exciton relaxation on the femtosecond timescale for excitons delocalized along the helical structure.
item.dc:creator: Indranil Ghosh, Keerthi Vaasan Mani, Caitlin C. Bellora, Gregory S. Engel

item.title: Observation of nonadiabatic quantum tunneling in a driven correlated insulator
item.description: arXiv:2611.28980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many emerging solid-state platforms for Floquet engineering, nonlinear transport, and high harmonic generation operate near the Keldysh crossover, where optical fields are sufficiently strong and fast to reshape electronic states on sub-cycle timescales. Despite its importance, the microscopic pathways for photocarrier generation in this regime remain poorly understood, as neither perturbative multiphoton absorption nor adiabatic tunneling provides an adequate description. Here, we perform time-resolved optical spectroscopy on the correlated van der Waals insulator NiPS$_3$ while systematically tuning the drive electric field and frequency over a wide range. In the crossover regime, we observe multiphoton-like resonances that are blue-shifted by ponderomotive effects within an otherwise tunneling-dominated absorption channel - a clear spectroscopic signature of adiabaticity breakdown. Hubbard-model simulations based on a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach qualitatively reproduce these features. Together, our results elucidate the microscopic mechanisms of charge excitation in the Keldysh crossover regime and identify a key ingredient for controlling strong-field nonlinear dynamics in correlated materials.
item.dc:creator: Mingyao Guo, Radu Andrei, Jaena Park, Je-Geun Park, Eugene Demler, David Hsieh

item.title: Improved two-way capacity upper bounds for amplitude-damping channels
item.description: arXiv:2611.29650v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We derive an improved upper bound on the two-way-assisted capacities of the qubit amplitude-damping channel with decay probability $\gamma$, given by $\log_2[1+(1-\gamma)\gamma^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)}]$. It applies to quantum communication, entanglement distribution, private communication, and secret-key agreement, and, for every $0<\gamma<1$, strictly improves the PLOB relative-entropy bound, the analytic max-relative-entropy bound, and the optimized balanced squashed-entanglement bound. At high damping, a known triple-rail protocol attains more than $99.54\%$ of its leading coefficient. Our method extends sector teleportation simulation to qubits: phase rotations and permutations give exact simulations within fixed-excitation subspaces while preserving the two-level input structure. We determine the exact, additive relative entropy of entanglement of the amplitude-damping resources and the exact regularized entanglement gain at fixed input population. We then derive explicit bounds for generalized amplitude damping, which includes thermal excitation. Combining the amplitude-damping gain with unital and entanglement-breaking channels gives a closed expression that recovers the zero-temperature result and vanishes throughout the entanglement-breaking region. It improves established benchmarks over broad parameter ranges, while the exact entanglement of the generalized resources remains open. Both results admit refinements under an average-excitation constraint. The bounds provide quantitative limits for adaptive communication through relaxing qubits and show how a sector simulation can remain useful beyond channels whose resource entanglement is known exactly.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Pirandola

item.title: Integrable discretization of the Maxwell-Bloch equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.30080v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Numerical schemes for the Maxwell-Bloch equations keep the length of the Bloch vector but not the integrable structure, so that solitons are only approximate solutions. We write an integrable discretization, in both time and space, of these equations for a complex field in a resonant two-level medium in the physical variables and use it as a numerical scheme. The lattice follows from a discrete Lax pair with the analytic structure of the continuous one; an auxiliary field variable is fixed by an isospectral normalization, and the resulting scheme is explicit, a $2\times2$ similarity transformation of the density matrix per grid node. It conserves the length of every Bloch vector and satisfies an exact energy balance between field and medium. The lattice coincides with a known fully discrete integrable system, which we use to obtain closed-form solitons and breathers; they are reflectionless potentials with energy $16\sum_j\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda_j$ and converge to the McCall-Hahn soliton and Lamb's breather. Inhomogeneous broadening is included through ordered sublayers that keep integrability. On a finite time window the scattering data evolve by a closed map, with the final state of the medium given by the data at one point of the spectral plane. On the infinite line, if the medium returns to its ground state behind the pulse (which we show on the first row and observe numerically on later rows), the transmission coefficient is conserved and the reflection coefficient evolves linearly, with the multiplier of the linearized lattice. As a numerical method the lattice is explicit and second order, with a cost per accuracy comparable to that of Cayley and exponential-midpoint schemes, and an area-preserving input map with a calibrated medium coupling makes it exact for a chosen soliton.
item.dc:creator: I. Kuk, I. Gabitov

item.title: Stellar Temporal Intensity Interferometry with Adaptive Optics at the Palomar Observatory
item.description: arXiv:2611.30257v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial intensity interferometry has seen a major resurgence in astronomy due to its immunity to atmospheric phase turbulence, but its temporal counterpart - a cornerstone of quantum optics - has remained largely unexplored for astronomical sources. Here, we demonstrate that high-visibility temporal photon bunching signatures from stellar sources are now accessible by combining ultra-narrowband spectral filtering with high-speed single-photon counting detectors. Leveraging the adaptive optics architecture at the Palomar Observatory, we report the first observation of resolved stellar temporal photon bunching, with a peak of $g^{(2)}(\tau=0) = 1.3 \pm 0.1$, from the red supergiant $\alpha$ Her. This advance establishes stellar temporal intensity interferometry as a viable observational modality, bridging quantum optics with high-resolution stellar astrophysics.
item.dc:creator: Darren Ming Zhi Koh, Xi Jie Yeo, Sam Halverson, Rebecca Oppenheimer, Gautam Vasisht, Christian Kurtsiefer, Peng Kian Tan

item.title: Femtosecond laser-controlled production of functional titanium niobate layers from TiO$_{2}$/Nb$_{2}$O$_{5}$ powders
item.description: arXiv:2611.30549v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional synthesis methods of titanium niobates (TNO) require prolongated high-temperature treatments. To overcome this limitation, in this work, we have developed a confined powder-bed femtosecond (fs) laser-based technique to sinter TNO films starting from a mixture of TiO$_{2}$ and Nb$_{2}$O$_{5}$ powders, avoiding furnace-based approaches. The influence of laser-processing conditions on film formation, phase composition, and microstructure is systematically investigated, demonstrating that different TNO phases and morphologies can be obtained by controlling the laser pulse energy. A comprehensive characterization of the processed films has been performed, providing insights into the mechanisms governing their formation, which appear to share key features with laser-induced backward transfer (LIBT) processes. Our findings establish the relationship between laser-processing conditions and TNO film formation, highlighting the potential of confined powder-bed fs-laser processing as an alternative route for manufacturing functional oxide layers. Tentative applications of these layers are finally discussed.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Gomez-Munoz, Aar\'on Calvo-Villoslada, Inmaculada \'Alvarez-Serrano, Mar\'ia Luisa L\'opez, Paloma Fern\'andez, Javier Solis, Bel\'en Sotillo

item.title: Geometry-conditioned differentiable surrogate with adjoint Monte Carlo sampling for scintillator detector co-design
item.description: arXiv:2611.30580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optimizing light-guide geometries for scintillator-based imaging detectors requires repeated photon-transport evaluations, making direct Monte Carlo simulation computationally costly. Differentiable surrogates can accelerate these evaluations and support detector readout co-design aimed at improving information extraction from particle interactions. In this work we describe a surrogate model for photon transport. We develop it starting from a modular, event-driven Monte Carlo model for the generation and transport of scintillation photons, and a reciprocal Monte Carlo construction (an adjoint model) of a spatially and temporally resolved optical response field. The latter evaluates the collectible light output and its temporal structure from a scintillator volume by launching weighted photon trajectories from the light-guide readout face. We apply this approach to a scintillator cell with two mirrored, curved, single-clad light guides. We employ the adjoint model to train a geometry-conditioned neural surrogate that predicts collection probabilities and conditional transport-time distributions across a constrained guide-design family. The surrogate is natively differentiable, lending itself to be an element of a differentiable pipeline for gradient-based optimization. A forward-reciprocal benchmark and validation on held-out geometries establish the accuracy of the trained model and identify its limitations. The developed tools provide a foundation for rapid optical-response studies and detector readout co-design.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Pepa, Mohammad Ali Marashli, Nicolas Babio Elguero, Tommaso Dorigo, Irene Fagnani, Carlo Gulizia, Pablo Martinez Ruiz del Arbol, Fredrik Sandin, Pietro Vischia

item.title: Twisted light affects ultrafast demagnetization
item.description: arXiv:2206.07502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Irradiation with an ultrashort laser pulse can completely destroy the magnetic order of ferromagnetic thin films on the femtosecond timescale. This phenomenon holds great potential for ultrafast spintronics and information processing and is an active field of research. It is still an open question if the angular momentum of light can support this effect. While it has been shown that the spin of light only has a negligible influence, we experimentally demonstrate the influence of photonic orbital angular momentum (OAM) on the magnetization dynamics of a thin nickel film. Our results reveal that the photonic OAM affects the demagnetization behavior by a non-coherent, secondary process within the first hundreds of femtoseconds depending on the handedness of the OAM with respect to the direction of the sample magnetization.
item.dc:creator: Eva Prinz, Paul Herrgen, Jonas Hoefer, Benjamin Stadtm\"uller, Martin Aeschlimann

item.title: Depth-multiplexing spectral domain OCT for full eye length imaging with a single modulation unit
item.description: arXiv:2311.17824v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clinical measurement of a patient's axial eye length is emerging as a crucial approach to track progression and monitor management of myopia. However, the preferred method for such measurements is swept-source OCT, whose cost prohibits broad use, especially in lower-income communities. Spectral domain (SD) OCT is a more affordable option, but it has limited imaging depth range, so is not suitable for full eye length measurement. Depth-multiplexing (DM) techniques for SD-OCT provide a workaround by capturing images at multiple depths within the eye. However, these methods typically require multiple light modulation units or detectors for simultaneous imaging across depths, adding complexity and cost. In response, we propose a novel DM-SD-OCT approach that utilizes a single light modulation unit for depth encoding. We capture images at multiple depths within the eye simultaneously with a single line scan camera, then computationally demix the contributions from different depths. Here, we demonstrate acquisition and demixing of signals from three distinct depths within the eye and validate experimentally in human subjects. Our method thus offers a cost-effective solution for comprehensive eye length measurement in clinical myopia research.

item.title: Incoherent Diffraction Imaging with a Pseudo-Thermal Light Source
item.description: arXiv:2501.05417v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Incoherent Diffraction Imaging - IDI - is a diffraction-based imaging technique that has been recently proposed to exploit the partial coherence of incoherently scattered light to retrieve structural information from the scattering centers. Similar to the stellar intensity interferometry of Hanbury Brown and Twiss, the signal builds up on the second-order spatial correlations of the emitted light. The complex spatial distribution of the target is thereby encoded in the spatial intensity fluctuations of the scattered light. The first experimental realisations of this imaging technique have been realised using the fluorescence excited by an ultra-short X-ray pulse at Free Electron Laser (FEL) facilities. Here, we propose an alternative set-up based on a table-top Pseudo-Thermal Light Source. This set-up allows us to explore IDI under a wide range of physically relevant conditions as well as to benchmark numerical and analytical models currently used to determine the imaging capabilities of this technique.

item.title: Fluctuation imaging of disorder in monolayer semiconductors
item.description: arXiv:2603.07418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Monolayer semiconductors hold great potential for nanoscale electronics, optoelectronics, and photonics. Excitons dominate their optical properties. As their electric fields extend outside the monolayer, they are sensitive to their surroundings. Thus, disorder can cause exciton instability, which is detrimental to device performance and critical for scalability and reproducibility. Here, we adapt a super-resolution fluorescence fluctuation microscopy technique to image localized exciton fluctuations in monolayer semiconductors, allowing us to identify unstable spots in an otherwise continuous monolayer with constant fluorescence. These spots correspond to interfacial disorder measured by atomic force microscopy. We examine how different material interfaces influence the fluctuations by comparing several substrates and provide additional insight into the disorder behind the fluctuations using hyperspectral imaging. We also assess the reduction of disorder upon thermal annealing, evidenced by a decrease in fluctuations. Our results show that fluorescence fluctuation imaging can detect disorder features similar to those of atomic force microscopy and hyperspectral imaging, while being faster and easier to implement. Therefore, it is a promising method for evaluating the quality of monolayer semiconductors, particularly when integrated with nanostructures and heterostructures found in nano-optoelectronic devices.
item.dc:creator: Tom T. C. Sistermans, Rasmus H. Godiksen, Sara A. Elrafei, Alberto G. Curto

item.title: Iterative approach for high-quality binary intensity hologram generation in augmented reality applications
item.description: arXiv:2604.11181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Binary amplitude spatial light modulators, such as digital micromirror devices (DMDs), are increasingly relevant for computer generated holography due to their high refresh rates, low cost, and due to the emergence of subwavelength pixel architectures. However, the binary constraint limits the reconstruction quality, as conventional approaches rely on a binarization applied as a final step after hologram computation which leads to reduced efficiency and contrast. We introduce an iterative estimation approach for the generation of off axis binary amplitude holograms, in which the binarization constraint is applied at each iteration. We validate the approach through numerical simulations and experimental reconstruction using a DMD based optical setup. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons with random superposition and Gerchberg Saxton methods demonstrate significant improvements in image contrast, light efficiency, and reconstruction fidelity, with comparable computational cost. The proposed method provides a practical route toward high quality CGH using binary modulators and supports emerging applications requiring high speed and high resolution holographic projection.

item.title: Thin-Film AlN Microbolometer for Very-Long-Wave Infrared Detection
item.description: arXiv:2604.22301v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We demonstrate a suspended thin-film aluminum nitride (AlN) microbolometer for narrowband very-long-wave infrared detection. The device uses a 100 nm-thick AlN membrane suspended above a Pt back reflector by a 1 $\mu$m air gap. Resonant absorption near 15.4 $\mu$m is set by the AlN transverse optical phonon and is strengthened by suspension above the reflector. A periodic perforation pattern reduces membrane thermal mass, facilitates release, and tunes the effective optical thickness without requiring a thinner deposited film. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) reflection measurements on the released bolometer show approximately 95% peak cavity absorptance near 15.4 $\mu$m with a 0.772 $\mu$m FWHM. DC resistance measurements under tunable infrared illumination verify bolometric operation, with a peak normalized resistive responsivity of 252 ppm/mW at 15.48 $\mu$m. This platform can enable compact wavelength-selective thermal detectors for multispectral imaging, on-chip infrared spectroscopy, and chemical sensing.

item.title: Dynamically Reconfigurable Optical Skyrmions Enabled by a Silicon Microring Optical Phased Array for Robust Free-Space Communication
item.description: arXiv:2605.10283v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical skyrmions can encode information in the skyrmion number for free-space communication through atmospheric turbulence. However, programming both the skyrmion number and type on a compact chip remains challenging. Here, we propose and numerically demonstrate a skyrmion generator based on a silicon optical phased array with optimized inner- and outer-grating microring emitters. The two emitter types provide orthogonal circularly polarized components and generate optical skyrmions through coherent superposition. The on-chip phase shifters configure the azimuthal phase distribution, enabling the $4\times4$ array to generate states with target skyrmion numbers of $-2$, $-1$, 1, and 2. Adjustment of the relative phase bias continuously switches states with target skyrmion numbers of $\pm1$ between the N\'eel and Bloch types. Increasing the array size to $12\times12$ extends the target range from $-8$ to 8. Laser wavelength tuning and calibration of the microring input phases and amplitudes recover target states within a range of simulated fabrication errors, which shows the robustness of the generator. Furthermore, we evaluate four-symbol communication using skyrmion-number decoding over a simulated 100 m turbulent link and observe no symbol errors in $10^4$ trials at Rytov variances up to 0.12. These results demonstrate the potential of this generator as a compact, programmable transmitter for turbulence-tolerant free-space optical communication.

item.title: Programmable Synthetic Motion at a Time-Varying Interface
item.description: arXiv:2606.13557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Space-time metamaterials that exhibit synthetic motion promise arbitrary control over the momentum, frequency and energy of scattered light, but realising the required space-time modulation in a programmable way remains a challenge. Here we program synthetic motion using a single spatial light modulator in a 4f geometry which imprints a continuously tunable pulse-front tilt onto a high-intensity pump pulse, inducing reflectivity modulations at a sub-wavelength indium tin oxide thin film with synthetic velocities spanning the sub- and superluminal regimes. The angle-resolved spectrum of a scattered probe pulse reveals space-time diffraction patterns whose gradient and bandwidth vary continuously with synthetic velocity, in excellent agreement with theory. Splitting the shaped pump into two independently controlled pulses yields space-time double-slit diffraction with tunable fringe separation and frequency-momentum gradient. This programmable platform opens a path towards non-linear and periodic space-time trajectories for tabletop analogue studies of relativistic phenomena and space-time metasurfaces.
